title: Final Verdict & My Recommendation
use_cases: Use when dialogue feels flat or thin in a work-in-progress
Implement when characters need to demonstrate emotional complexity through subtext
Configure when revising a specific scene to increase dramatic tension
Use when planning character movements and gestures during conversational scenes
content:
This experiment reaffirmed a core belief I’ve held since my first literature seminar: what is not said is often the most important part of any story.

If you’re a writer whose dialogue feels thin, I implore you to try this. Take one scene from your work-in-progress. A scene that feels flat. Print it out. And then, go through these seven methods, one by one. You don’t have to use all of them, but use them as a checklist of possibilities. Ask yourself: “How can my character avoid answering this question? What would they do with their hands while they lie? What do they really mean when they say ‘I’m fine’?”

Let your characters be evasive, difficult, and indirect. Let them be human. You will be astonished at the truth they finally tell.
